replacement: If anyone could point out a middle position between the complete independence and the complete subjection of public expression of opinion, and one that could actually be held, I should perhaps be inclined to adopt it. But the difficulty is to find such a position. Suppose you want to correct the abuses of an unlicensed press and restore the use of orderly language. You may begin by trying the offender before a jury. But if the jury acquits him, the opinion of a single individual becomes the opinion of the whole country. So far, then, too much has been done, and too little. If you go further, you must bring the offender before a court of permanent judges. But even there the case must be heard before it can be decided, and the very principles that no book would have dared to avow are proclaimed aloud in the pleadings. What was hinted at obscurely in a single work is then repeated in a multitude of other publications. The words in which a thought is expressed are only the body of the thought, not the idea itself. Tribunals may condemn the form, but the sense and spirit of the work are too subtle for their authority. Too much has been done to turn back, and too little to reach your goal, so you must go on. If you establish a censorship of the press, the public speaker will still be heard, and you have only made the mischief worse. The powers of thought do not depend, as physical strength does, on the number of their mechanical agents, and you cannot count a host of authors the way you count the troops of an army. On the contrary, the authority of a principle is often increased by how few men express it. The words of a strong-minded man, reaching into the passions of a listening assembly, have more power than the shouting of a thousand orators. And if free speech is allowed in any one public place, the result is the same as if it were allowed in every village. The liberty of speech must therefore be destroyed as well as the liberty of the press. That is the necessary end of your efforts. But if your aim was to repress the abuses of liberty, they have brought you to the feet of a despot. You have been driven from the extreme of independence to the extreme of subjection without finding a single position along the way where you could take shelter or rest.

In America there is hardly a hamlet that does not have its own newspaper. It is easy to see that neither discipline nor unity of purpose can be imposed on so numerous and varied a host, and so each paper fights under its own banner. All the political journals of the United States are indeed lined up on the side of the administration or against it, but they attack and defend in a thousand different ways. They cannot succeed in forming those great currents of opinion that overwhelm the most solid obstacles. This division of the press’s influence produces a number of other consequences that are almost as remarkable. The ease with which journals can be started draws a multitude of people into them. But because the amount of competition rules out any considerable profit, the most distinguished classes of society are rarely drawn to these undertakings. Yet there are so many public prints that, even if they were a source of wealth, writers of ability could not be found to run them all. The journalists of the United States are usually in a very humble position, with little education and a vulgar turn of mind. The will of the majority is the most general of laws, and it establishes certain habits that form the characteristics of each particular class of society. In this way it dictates the etiquette practiced at courts and the etiquette of the bar. The French journalist is characterized by a violent, though often eloquent and lofty, manner of discussing the politics of the day, and exceptions to this habit are only occasional. The American journalist is characterized by an open and coarse appeal to the passions of the populace. He habitually abandons the principles of political science to attack the characters of individuals, to follow them into private life, and to expose all their weaknesses and faults.

When the liberty of the press acts on men in the first of these three states, it does not immediately disturb their habit of believing without question or investigation, but it constantly changes the objects of their intuitive convictions. The human mind continues to see only one point on the whole intellectual horizon, and that point is always moving. Such are the symptoms of sudden revolutions, and of the misfortunes that are sure to befall those generations that abruptly adopt unconditional freedom of the press.
